L05 · Regression & Regularization

L05 · Regression — Linear, Polynomial and Regularization

Lecture 5 (slides "Regression, Linear, Polynomial, and Regularization", 46 pages) · Bishop PRML §1.1 · Deisenroth Ch. 9

Lecture 5 slides (PDF) Revision notes: Linear & polynomial regression Revision notes: Ridge & lasso Problem Set 5 PSet 5 solutions Problem Set 6 (P1–P2 ridge) PSet 6 solutions Worksheet 3 Read them all on this page ↓
Exam pattern: Mid-exam information (slide 2)

Date and time: 18 October, 9 am – 12 pm. Venue: SDSB-B3.
Part 1: multiple-choice and/or short questions, 45 minutes. Part 2: problems, 90–120 minutes. See the Mid guide.

This lecture builds the course's second learning algorithm and the template for most of what follows. In order, it covers: the regression set-up of process, noise, model and error; the four-step modular recipe; what "linear" means, with the fitness-tracker example; the loss functions LSE, MSE and RMSE and why they share a minimiser; the closed-form least-squares solution, derived twice — by calculus and by orthogonal projection — together with the conditions under which it exists; polynomial regression as linear regression in disguise; underfitting, overfitting and their three remedies in Bishop's sine example; bias and variance; and regularization — ridge regression with its closed form and geometry, the lasso and its sparsity, the elastic net — and how to choose the penalty.

#1. The regression set-up

🧩Background you needfunctions, noise and models

A function is a rule that turns an input into an output, such as f(x)=4.2+2.4xf(x)=4.2+2.4xf(x)=4.2+2.4x: input x=1x=1x=1 gives 6.66.66.6.

Noise. Real measurements never sit exactly on a neat rule. Two 40-year-olds may exercise 3 and 5 hours a week; age alone cannot explain the difference. We write the observed value as "rule plus a random wobble":
y=f(x)+n.y=f(x)+n .y=f(x)+n.
A model is our guess at the unknown rule fff. We pick its shape in advance (for example, a straight line θ0+θ1x\theta_0+\theta_1xθ0​+θ1​x) and then choose the numbers θ0,θ1\theta_0,\theta_1θ0​,θ1​ — the parameters — to fit the data as well as possible.

The error (residual) for one data point is the vertical gap between what was observed and what the model predicts: e=y−y^e=y-\hat ye=y−y^​.

Regression is quantitative prediction on a continuous scale: given a data sample, predict a numerical value. We picture the data as produced by an unknown process corrupted by noise:
x ⟶  process or system f(x)  ⟶ ⊕ ⟵ n  (noise),y=f(x)+n.x\ \longrightarrow\ \boxed{\ \text{process or system } f(x)\ }\ \longrightarrow\ \oplus\ \longleftarrow\ n\ \ (\text{noise}), \qquad\qquad y=f(x)+n .x ⟶  process or system f(x) ​ ⟶ ⊕ ⟵ n  (noise),y=f(x)+n.
Here the process or system is whatever physical or logical phenomenon maps the inputs to the observed, noisy outputs. The true model is an inherent but unknown relationship fff between input and output. The goal is to estimate that unknown functional relationship, as accurately as possible, from noisy observations. (Two customers of the same age may exercise three and five hours a week: age cannot explain everything, and the noise nnn stands for all that we did not measure.)

Term Meaning
one-variable regression the output yyy is a scalar (covered in this course)
multi-variable regression the output y\mathbf yy is a vector
single-feature regression the input xxx is a scalar (covered)
multiple-feature regression the input x\mathbf xx is a vector (covered)

Examples. With a single feature: a course score from the hours of effort per week, or monthly e-commerce sales from advertising spend. With several features: machine efficiency from temperature and vibration sensors; the remaining useful life of a battery from its charging and discharging history; sales volume from demographics, GDP and climate; crop yield from satellite and gravity data; surge pricing in ride-hailing; driver fatigue from video; and driving quality from in-car sensors.

Formulating the model. The training data are D={(x1,y1),…,(xn,yn)}⊆Xd×YD=\{(x_1,y_1),\dots,(x_n,y_n)\}\subseteq\mathcal X^d\times\mathcal YD={(x1​,y1​),…,(xn​,yn​)}⊆Xd×Y; the slide's example uses the true function f(x)=4.2+2.4xf(x)=4.2+2.4xf(x)=4.2+2.4x. Our model y^=f^(x,θ)\hat y=\hat f(x,\theta)y^​=f^​(x,θ) has two ingredients: a structure chosen in advance (linear, polynomial, inverse, …) and parameters θ=[θ1,…,θM]\theta=[\theta_1,\dots,\theta_M]θ=[θ1​,…,θM​] tuned from the data. The model error is e=y−y^e=y-\hat ye=y−y^​.

Definition: The modular recipe

Linear regression is the course's second learning algorithm and, unlike kNN, it is modular. Almost every later method follows the same four steps:

  1. Select a model.
  2. Define a loss function that measures how badly the model fits the data.
  3. Formulate an optimisation problem: find the parameters that minimise the loss.
  4. Solve it, either analytically (set the derivative to zero) or numerically (an algorithm that moves step by step towards the minimiser).
Remember

y=f(x)+ny=f(x)+ny=f(x)+n: we never see fff, only noisy samples of it; we choose a model structure and a loss, and then optimise the parameters.

#2. The linear model

🧩Background you needbuilding the design matrix by hand

A line y^=w0+w1x\hat y=w_0+w_1xy^​=w0​+w1​x: w0w_0w0​ is where the line crosses the vertical axis (the intercept) and w1w_1w1​ is how much y^\hat yy^​ rises when xxx rises by 111 (the slope).

Why the column of ones? We want to write all the predictions as one matrix product. The trick is to treat the intercept as "w0w_0w0​ times 111":
y^i=w0⋅1+w1xi.\hat y_i=w_0\cdot1+w_1x_i .y^​i​=w0​⋅1+w1​xi​.
For the four customers aged 25,30,40,5025,30,40,5025,30,40,50:
[y^1y^2y^3y^4]=[w0⋅1+w1⋅25w0⋅1+w1⋅30w0⋅1+w1⋅40w0⋅1+w1⋅50]=[125130140150]⏟X[w0w1].\begin{bmatrix}\hat y_1\\ \hat y_2\\ \hat y_3\\ \hat y_4\end{bmatrix} =\begin{bmatrix}w_0\cdot1+w_1\cdot25\\ w_0\cdot1+w_1\cdot30\\ w_0\cdot1+w_1\cdot40\\ w_0\cdot1+w_1\cdot50\end{bmatrix} =\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1&25\\1&30\\1&40\\1&50\end{bmatrix}}_{X}\begin{bmatrix}w_0\\w_1\end{bmatrix}.​y^​1​y^​2​y^​3​y^​4​​​=​w0​⋅1+w1​⋅25w0​⋅1+w1​⋅30w0​⋅1+w1​⋅40w0​⋅1+w1​⋅50​​=X​1111​25304050​​​​[w0​w1​​].
Each row of XXX is "111, then that person's features". With two features, each row becomes (1, age, sleep)(1,\ \text{age},\ \text{sleep})(1, age, sleep) and www gets a third entry.

Definition: What "linear" means

d=1:f^(x,θ)=θ0+θ1x(a line),d=2:f^(x,θ)=θ0+θ1x1+θ2x2(a plane),general d:f^(x,θ)=θ0+∑i=1dθixi=θ0+θ⊤x(a hyperplane in Rd+1).\begin{aligned} d=1:&\quad \hat f(x,\theta)=\theta_0+\theta_1x &&(\text{a line}),\\ d=2:&\quad \hat f(x,\theta)=\theta_0+\theta_1x_1+\theta_2x_2 &&(\text{a plane}),\\ \text{general } d:&\quad \hat f(x,\theta)=\theta_0+\sum_{i=1}^d\theta_ix_i=\theta_0+\theta^\top x &&(\text{a hyperplane in }\mathbb{R}^{d+1}). \end{aligned}d=1:d=2:general d:​f^​(x,θ)=θ0​+θ1​xf^​(x,θ)=θ0​+θ1​x1​+θ2​x2​f^​(x,θ)=θ0​+i=1∑d​θi​xi​=θ0​+θ⊤x​​(a line),(a plane),(a hyperplane in Rd+1).​
The parameter θ0\theta_0θ0​ is the bias or intercept; θ=[θ1,…,θd]\theta=[\theta_1,\dots,\theta_d]θ=[θ1​,…,θd​] are the weights or slopes; and θi\theta_iθi​ measures the contribution of feature xix_ixi​. There are d+1d+1d+1 parameters in all. Different choices give different hyperplanes, which raises the question: how do we find the "best" one, and what does "best" mean?

Matrix form. Treat the intercept as the weight of an extra feature that always equals 111, and stack the nnn predictions:
[y^1y^2⋮y^n]⏟y^=[1x1⊤1x2⊤⋮⋮1xn⊤]⏟X∈Rn×(d+1)[θ0θ]⏟w.\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}\hat y_1\\ \hat y_2\\ \vdots\\ \hat y_n\end{bmatrix}}_{\hat{\mathbf y}} =\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1&x_1^\top\\1&x_2^\top\\ \vdots&\vdots\\1&x_n^\top\end{bmatrix}}_{X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times(d+1)}} \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}\theta_0\\ \theta\end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf w}.y^​​y^​1​y^​2​⋮y^​n​​​​​=X∈Rn×(d+1)​11⋮1​x1⊤​x2⊤​⋮xn⊤​​​​​w[θ0​θ​]​​.
The matrix XXX is the design matrix: one row per sample, one column per feature, plus the leading column of ones. Always write down the shapes first. With 100100100 customers and 555 features, XXX is 100×6100\times6100×6, www is 6×16\times16×1, and X⊤XX^\top XX⊤X is 6×66\times66×6.

#3. The loss function

🧩Background you needwhy a squared length is e⊤ee^\top ee⊤e

One error squared: ei2e_i^2ei2​. All of them added up: e12+e22+⋯+en2e_1^2+e_2^2+\cdots+e_n^2e12​+e22​+⋯+en2​.

From L01, that sum is exactly the squared length of the error vector, and also the inner product of the error vector with itself:
e12+⋯+en2=∥e∥2=e⊤e.e_1^2+\cdots+e_n^2=\|e\|^2=e^\top e .e12​+⋯+en2​=∥e∥2=e⊤e.
And the error vector is "observed minus predicted", e=y−Xwe=y-Xwe=y−Xw. Putting the two together,
∑i=1n(yi−y^i)2=∥y−Xw∥2.\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\hat y_i)^2=\|y-Xw\|^2 .i=1∑n​(yi​−y^​i​)2=∥y−Xw∥2.
So "make the total squared error small" is the same as "make the vector XwXwXw close to the vector yyy".

The loss must be a function of the model parameters. For an input xxx, the residual error is
e=y−y^=y−θ0−θ⊤x,e=y-\hat y=y-\theta_0-\theta^\top x ,e=y−y^​=y−θ0​−θ⊤x,
which is the vertical gap between the observed value and the fitted line.

Definition: Three squared losses with one minimiser

LSE=∑i=1n(yi−θ0−θ⊤xi)2,MSE=1n∑i=1n(yi−θ0−θ⊤xi)2,RMSE=1n∑i=1n(yi−θ0−θ⊤xi)2.\text{LSE}=\sum_{i=1}^n\big(y_i-\theta_0-\theta^\top x_i\big)^2, \qquad \text{MSE}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\big(y_i-\theta_0-\theta^\top x_i\big)^2, \qquad \text{RMSE}=\sqrt{\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\big(y_i-\theta_0-\theta^\top x_i\big)^2}.LSE=i=1∑n​(yi​−θ0​−θ⊤xi​)2,MSE=n1​i=1∑n​(yi​−θ0​−θ⊤xi​)2,RMSE=n1​i=1∑n​(yi​−θ0​−θ⊤xi​)2​.
Dividing by nnn and taking a square root are both increasing operations, so all three losses have the same minimiser. We therefore solve the unconstrained problem
minimizeθ0, θL(θ0,θ)=12∑i=1n(yi−θ0−θ⊤xi)2,\underset{\theta_0,\,\theta}{\text{minimize}}\quad \mathcal L(\theta_0,\theta)=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n\big(y_i-\theta_0-\theta^\top x_i\big)^2 ,θ0​,θminimize​L(θ0​,θ)=21​i=1∑n​(yi​−θ0​−θ⊤xi​)2,
where the factor 12\tfrac1221​ is a mathematical convenience: it cancels the 222 produced by differentiation.

Why squares? A plain sum of residuals would let positive and negative errors cancel. Squares remove the sign; they punish large errors more heavily (an error of 444 costs sixteen times an error of 111); they are smooth, unlike ∣e∣|e|∣e∣, which has a kink at 000; they lead to a clean formula; and, as the probability part of the course will show, they are the natural loss when the noise is Gaussian.

How to solve the problem? Analytically, by finding the critical point where the derivative (if it exists) is zero; or numerically, by an algorithm that iteratively approaches the minimiser.

Reformulation in vector form. Stack the residuals ei=yi−θ0−xi⊤θe_i=y_i-\theta_0-x_i^\top\thetaei​=yi​−θ0​−xi⊤​θ into a vector:
[e1⋮en]=[y1⋮yn]−[1x1⊤⋮⋮1xn⊤][θ0θ],that is,e=y−Xw.\begin{bmatrix}e_1\\ \vdots\\ e_n\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}y_1\\ \vdots\\ y_n\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1&x_1^\top\\ \vdots&\vdots\\1&x_n^\top\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\theta_0\\ \theta\end{bmatrix}, \qquad\text{that is,}\qquad e=y-Xw .​e1​⋮en​​​=​y1​⋮yn​​​−​1⋮1​x1⊤​⋮xn⊤​​​[θ0​θ​],that is,e=y−Xw.
The loss then takes the compact form
L(w)=12 e⊤e=12 (y−Xw)⊤(y−Xw)=12 ∥y−Xw∥22.\mathcal L(w)=\tfrac12\,e^\top e=\tfrac12\,(y-Xw)^\top(y-Xw)=\tfrac12\,\|y-Xw\|_2^2 .L(w)=21​e⊤e=21​(y−Xw)⊤(y−Xw)=21​∥y−Xw∥22​.
In the slide's words, this is a "very beautiful, elegant function": fitting the model means making XwXwXw as close as possible to yyy in Euclidean distance.

Remember

LSE, MSE and RMSE share a single minimiser; write the loss as 12∥y−Xw∥22\tfrac12\|y-Xw\|_2^221​∥y−Xw∥22​ with residual e=y−Xwe=y-Xwe=y−Xw.

#4. The closed-form solution

🧩Background you needderivatives, partial derivatives and the gradient — from scratch

Derivatives of one variable

The derivative f′(x)f'(x)f′(x) is the slope of fff at xxx. At the bottom of a valley the slope is zero, which is how we find minimum points. The rules you need:
ddxc=0,ddx(ax)=a,ddx(ax2)=2ax,ddx(12ax2)=ax.\frac{d}{dx}c=0,\qquad \frac{d}{dx}(ax)=a,\qquad \frac{d}{dx}(ax^2)=2ax,\qquad \frac{d}{dx}\big(\tfrac12ax^2\big)=ax .dxd​c=0,dxd​(ax)=a,dxd​(ax2)=2ax,dxd​(21​ax2)=ax.
Example. f(w)=(w−3)2=w2−6w+9f(w)=(w-3)^2=w^2-6w+9f(w)=(w−3)2=w2−6w+9 has f′(w)=2w−6f'(w)=2w-6f′(w)=2w−6, which is zero at w=3w=3w=3 — the bottom of the parabola.

Partial derivatives

When a function has several inputs, ∂f∂x1\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}∂x1​∂f​ is the slope in the x1x_1x1​ direction: treat every other variable as a constant and differentiate as usual.
f(x1,x2)=x12+3x1x2+5x2⟹∂f∂x1=2x1+3x2,∂f∂x2=3x1+5.f(x_1,x_2)=x_1^2+3x_1x_2+5x_2\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}=2x_1+3x_2,\qquad \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2}=3x_1+5 .f(x1​,x2​)=x12​+3x1​x2​+5x2​⟹∂x1​∂f​=2x1​+3x2​,∂x2​∂f​=3x1​+5.

The gradient

The gradient ∇f\nabla f∇f stacks all the partial derivatives into one vector:
∇f=[∂f/∂x1∂f/∂x2]=[2x1+3x23x1+5].\nabla f=\begin{bmatrix}\partial f/\partial x_1\\ \partial f/\partial x_2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2x_1+3x_2\\3x_1+5\end{bmatrix}.∇f=[∂f/∂x1​∂f/∂x2​​]=[2x1​+3x2​3x1​+5​].
At a minimum of a smooth function, every slope is zero, so ∇f=0\nabla f=\mathbf 0∇f=0. Solving ∇f=0\nabla f=\mathbf 0∇f=0 is the vector version of solving f′(x)=0f'(x)=0f′(x)=0.

A transpose fact used in the expansion

A 1×11\times11×1 matrix is just a number, and a number equals its own transpose. Since y⊤Xwy^\top Xwy⊤Xw is a single number, y⊤Xw=(y⊤Xw)⊤=w⊤X⊤yy^\top Xw=(y^\top Xw)^\top=w^\top X^\top yy⊤Xw=(y⊤Xw)⊤=w⊤X⊤y.

#4a. By calculus (slides p25–27)

Step 1 — expand the loss. Using (Xw)⊤=w⊤X⊤(Xw)^\top=w^\top X^\top(Xw)⊤=w⊤X⊤,
L(w)=12(y⊤y−y⊤Xw−w⊤X⊤y+w⊤X⊤Xw).\mathcal L(w)=\tfrac12\big(y^\top y-y^\top Xw-w^\top X^\top y+w^\top X^\top Xw\big).L(w)=21​(y⊤y−y⊤Xw−w⊤X⊤y+w⊤X⊤Xw).
The two middle terms are scalars, and a scalar equals its own transpose, so y⊤Xw=(y⊤Xw)⊤=w⊤X⊤yy^\top Xw=(y^\top Xw)^\top=w^\top X^\top yy⊤Xw=(y⊤Xw)⊤=w⊤X⊤y. Hence
L(w)=12(y⊤y−2 w⊤X⊤y+w⊤X⊤Xw).\mathcal L(w)=\tfrac12\big(y^\top y-2\,w^\top X^\top y+w^\top X^\top Xw\big).L(w)=21​(y⊤y−2w⊤X⊤y+w⊤X⊤Xw).

Definition: The gradient

For a function f:Rd→Rf:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}f:Rd→R, the gradient is the vector of partial derivatives,
∇f(x)=[∂f∂x1, ∂f∂x2, …, ∂f∂xd]⊤∈Rd,\nabla f(x)=\left[\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1},\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2},\ \dots,\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_d}\right]^\top\in\mathbb{R}^d ,∇f(x)=[∂x1​∂f​, ∂x2​∂f​, …, ∂xd​∂f​]⊤∈Rd,
which records the rate of change of fff along each direction; it is the zero vector at a flat point. Three rules are needed:
∇(a⊤x)=∇(x⊤a)=a,∇(x⊤x)=2x,∇(x⊤Px)=2Pxfor symmetric P\nabla\big(a^\top x\big)=\nabla\big(x^\top a\big)=a,\qquad \nabla\big(x^\top x\big)=2x,\qquad \nabla\big(x^\top Px\big)=2Px\quad\text{for symmetric }P∇(a⊤x)=∇(x⊤a)=a,∇(x⊤x)=2x,∇(x⊤Px)=2Pxfor symmetric P
(for a general PPP the last gradient is (P+P⊤)x(P+P^\top)x(P+P⊤)x).

Derivation: The gradient of a quadratic (PSet 5, Problem 1)

The claim. If f(x)=12x⊤Ax+b⊤xf(x)=\tfrac12x^\top Ax+b^\top xf(x)=21​x⊤Ax+b⊤x with AAA symmetric, then ∇f(x)=Ax+b\nabla f(x)=Ax+b∇f(x)=Ax+b. This is the vector version of the school rule ddx(12ax2+bx)=ax+b\frac{d}{dx}\big(\tfrac12ax^2+bx\big)=ax+bdxd​(21​ax2+bx)=ax+b.

Step 1 — see it in two dimensions. Take
A=[accd] (symmetric),b=[b1b2],x=[x1x2].A=\begin{bmatrix}a&c\\c&d\end{bmatrix}\ (\text{symmetric}),\qquad b=\begin{bmatrix}b_1\\b_2\end{bmatrix},\qquad x=\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\x_2\end{bmatrix}.A=[ac​cd​] (symmetric),b=[b1​b2​​],x=[x1​x2​​].
Multiply out the quadratic form: first AxAxAx, then x⊤(Ax)x^\top(Ax)x⊤(Ax).
Ax=[ax1+cx2cx1+dx2],x⊤Ax=x1(ax1+cx2)+x2(cx1+dx2)=ax12+2c x1x2+dx22.Ax=\begin{bmatrix}ax_1+cx_2\\cx_1+dx_2\end{bmatrix},\qquad x^\top Ax=x_1(ax_1+cx_2)+x_2(cx_1+dx_2)=ax_1^2+2c\,x_1x_2+dx_2^2 .Ax=[ax1​+cx2​cx1​+dx2​​],x⊤Ax=x1​(ax1​+cx2​)+x2​(cx1​+dx2​)=ax12​+2cx1​x2​+dx22​.
So fff is an ordinary function of two numbers:
f(x1,x2)=12(ax12+2c x1x2+dx22)+b1x1+b2x2.f(x_1,x_2)=\tfrac12\big(ax_1^2+2c\,x_1x_2+dx_2^2\big)+b_1x_1+b_2x_2 .f(x1​,x2​)=21​(ax12​+2cx1​x2​+dx22​)+b1​x1​+b2​x2​.
Take each partial derivative, treating the other variable as a constant:

#4b. By orthogonal projection — no calculus (outline, Week 4)

Every prediction vector XwXwXw lies in the column space C(X)\mathcal C(X)C(X) (L03), while yyy, for a tall XXX, usually does not. The point of C(X)\mathcal C(X)C(X) closest to yyy is the orthogonal projection y^\hat yy^​, and the defining property of an orthogonal projection is that the error e=y−y^e=y-\hat ye=y−y^​ is orthogonal to every column of XXX:
X⊤(y−Xw)=0⟺X⊤Xw=X⊤y.X^\top(y-Xw)=\mathbf 0\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad X^\top Xw=X^\top y .X⊤(y−Xw)=0⟺X⊤Xw=X⊤y.
These are the same normal equations, obtained this time by geometry alone.

Why the projection is the closest point. Take any other point p=Xv∈C(X)p=Xv\in\mathcal C(X)p=Xv∈C(X). Then
y−p=(y−y^)⏟e+(y^−p)⏟∈ C(X),y-p=\underbrace{(y-\hat y)}_{e}+\underbrace{(\hat y-p)}_{\in\,\mathcal C(X)},y−p=e(y−y^​)​​+∈C(X)(y^​−p)​​,
and the two pieces are orthogonal, so Pythagoras gives
∥y−p∥2=∥e∥2+∥y^−p∥2 ≥ ∥e∥2.\|y-p\|^2=\|e\|^2+\|\hat y-p\|^2\ \ge\ \|e\|^2 .∥y−p∥2=∥e∥2+∥y^​−p∥2 ≥ ∥e∥2.
The course derives least squares twice on purpose; the calculus derivation returns once more in L08.

The projection matrix. The fitted values are y^=X(X⊤X)−1X⊤y=Py\hat y=X(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y=Pyy^​=X(X⊤X)−1X⊤y=Py, where P=X(X⊤X)−1X⊤P=X(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\topP=X(X⊤X)−1X⊤ is symmetric and satisfies P2=PP^2=PP2=P. For a single column uuu it reduces to P=uu⊤u⊤uP=\dfrac{uu^\top}{u^\top u}P=u⊤uuu⊤​, the vector projection of L01.

Two sanity checks. Because the first column of XXX is the vector of ones, the condition 1⊤e=0\mathbf 1^\top e=01⊤e=0 says that the residuals sum to zero, and it follows that the fitted line passes through the point of averages (xˉ,yˉ)(\bar x,\bar y)(xˉ,yˉ​).

#4c. It is a minimum, and when the inverse exists

The Hessian — the matrix of second derivatives — of L\mathcal LL is X⊤XX^\top XX⊤X, and for every vvv
v⊤X⊤Xv=∥Xv∥22 ≥ 0.v^\top X^\top Xv=\|Xv\|_2^2\ \ge\ 0 .v⊤X⊤Xv=∥Xv∥22​ ≥ 0.
The loss therefore curves upwards in every direction; it is a bowl, and its flat point is the global minimum.

X⊤XX^\top XX⊤X is invertible exactly when the columns of XXX are linearly independent (the Gram-matrix argument of L02). This fails in two situations:

  • too little data: we need n≥d+1n\ge d+1n≥d+1, at least as many samples as parameters;
  • redundant features: if a column is a combination of others — height in centimetres and in metres, or feature 505050 equal to twice feature 333 — then X⊤XX^\top XX⊤X is singular and there is a whole line or plane of equally good www.

The remedies are to remove the redundant feature or to regularise (§9).

Treat it like (a−b)(a−b)=a2−ab−ba+b2(a-b)(a-b)=a^2-ab-ba+b^2(a−b)(a−b)=a2−ab−ba+b2, keeping the order of the matrix products.

Step 2 — multiply the four pairs:
(y⊤−w⊤X⊤)(y−Xw)=y⊤y−y⊤Xw−w⊤X⊤y+w⊤X⊤Xw.(y^\top-w^\top X^\top)(y-Xw)=y^\top y-y^\top Xw-w^\top X^\top y+w^\top X^\top Xw .(y⊤−w⊤X⊤)(y−Xw)=y⊤y−y⊤Xw−w⊤X⊤y+w⊤X⊤Xw.

=y⊤y−2 w⊤X⊤y+w⊤(X⊤X) w.=y^\top y-2\,w^\top X^\top y+w^\top(X^\top X)\,w .=y⊤y−2w⊤X⊤y+w⊤(X⊤X)w.
This has the shape "constant −-− (linear in www) +++ (quadratic in www)" — a bowl — so it has a lowest point.

🔍Where does this come from?from the gradient to the normal equations

Differentiate the three terms of L(w)=12(y⊤y−2w⊤X⊤y+w⊤X⊤Xw)\mathcal L(w)=\tfrac12\big(y^\top y-2w^\top X^\top y+w^\top X^\top Xw\big)L(w)=21​(y⊤y−2w⊤X⊤y+w⊤X⊤Xw):

  • y⊤yy^\top yy⊤y contains no www, so its gradient is 0\mathbf 00 (like the derivative of a constant).
  • w⊤(X⊤y)w^\top(X^\top y)w⊤(X⊤y) is "vector ⋅\cdot⋅ www", like a wa\,waw; its gradient is the vector X⊤yX^\top yX⊤y (like ddwaw=a\frac{d}{dw}aw=adwd​aw=a).
  • w⊤(X⊤X)ww^\top(X^\top X)ww⊤(X⊤X)w is the matrix version of a w2a\,w^2aw2; its gradient is 2X⊤Xw2X^\top Xw2X⊤Xw (like ddwaw2=2aw\frac{d}{dw}aw^2=2awdwd​aw2=2aw). See the box on the gradient of a quadratic.

So
∇L=12(0−2X⊤y+2X⊤Xw)=X⊤Xw−X⊤y.\nabla\mathcal L=\tfrac12\big(\mathbf 0-2X^\top y+2X^\top Xw\big)=X^\top Xw-X^\top y .∇L=21​(0−2X⊤y+2X⊤Xw)=X⊤Xw−X⊤y.
Setting it to zero gives X⊤Xw=X⊤yX^\top Xw=X^\top yX⊤Xw=X⊤y. If X⊤XX^\top XX⊤X has an inverse, multiply both sides on the left by it:
w=(X⊤X)−1X⊤y.w=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y .w=(X⊤X)−1X⊤y.
A one-variable sanity check. With a single feature and no intercept, X⊤X=∑xi2X^\top X=\sum x_i^2X⊤X=∑xi2​ and X⊤y=∑xiyiX^\top y=\sum x_iy_iX⊤y=∑xi​yi​ are numbers, and the formula says w=∑xiyi∑xi2w=\dfrac{\sum x_iy_i}{\sum x_i^2}w=∑xi2​∑xi​yi​​ — the slope of the best line through the origin.

🔍Where does this come from?the projection argument, in pictures

Every possible prediction XwXwXw lies in the column space of XXX (L03) — think of it as a flat sheet. The target yyy is usually off the sheet.

The closest point of the sheet to yyy is found the way you find the closest point of a floor to a lamp: drop a perpendicular. The error arrow e=y−Xwe=y-Xwe=y−Xw must then be perpendicular to the sheet, which means perpendicular to every column of XXX:
(column j)⊤e=0 for every j⟺X⊤e=0⟺X⊤(y−Xw)=0.(\text{column }j)^\top e=0\ \text{for every }j\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad X^\top e=\mathbf 0\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad X^\top(y-Xw)=\mathbf 0 .(column j)⊤e=0 for every j⟺X⊤e=0⟺X⊤(y−Xw)=0.
Multiplying out the last form gives the normal equations again, X⊤Xw=X⊤yX^\top Xw=X^\top yX⊤Xw=X⊤y — no calculus needed.

Remember

Least squares solves X⊤Xw=X⊤yX^\top Xw=X^\top yX⊤Xw=X⊤y, giving w=(X⊤X)−1X⊤yw=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top yw=(X⊤X)−1X⊤y — derived either by setting ∇L=0\nabla\mathcal L=\mathbf 0∇L=0 or by requiring the residual to be orthogonal to C(X)\mathcal C(X)C(X) — and it requires independent columns.

The residuals are 19(−2, 1, 3, −2)\tfrac19(-2,\ 1,\ 3,\ -2)91​(−2, 1, 3, −2) and the total squared error is 2/9≈0.222/9\approx0.222/9≈0.22.

A warning. The negative weight on sleep is not believable. Age and sleep have correlation about −0.92-0.92−0.92 in these data, so the model cannot separate their effects. Moreover, adding a feature can never increase the training error (the smaller model is the special case w2=0w_2=0w2​=0), so a lower training error is not evidence that the feature helps; and fitting three parameters to four points leaves very little protection against noise.

#6. Polynomial regression

🧩Background you needpolynomials and 'linear in the parameters'

A polynomial of degree MMM is a sum of powers: θ0+θ1x+θ2x2+⋯+θMxM\theta_0+\theta_1x+\theta_2x^2+\cdots+\theta_Mx^Mθ0​+θ1​x+θ2​x2+⋯+θM​xM. Degree 111 is a line, degree 222 a parabola, and so on.

The key idea. Treat each power of xxx as if it were a separate feature. For the data point x=3x=3x=3, the "features" are
(1, x, x2, x3)=(1, 3, 9, 27).(1,\ x,\ x^2,\ x^3)=(1,\ 3,\ 9,\ 27).(1, x, x2, x3)=(1, 3, 9, 27).
The prediction θ0⋅1+θ1⋅3+θ2⋅9+θ3⋅27\theta_0\cdot1+\theta_1\cdot3+\theta_2\cdot9+\theta_3\cdot27θ0​⋅1+θ1​⋅3+θ2​⋅9+θ3​⋅27 is a plain weighted sum of these numbers — exactly the linear model of §2. The curve is bent in xxx, but the parameters θ\thetaθ still appear only multiplied by known numbers and added up. That is all least squares needs, so the same formula θ=(X⊤X)−1X⊤y\theta=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top yθ=(X⊤X)−1X⊤y applies, with one column of XXX per power.

Overview. When the relationship between the inputs and the output is not linear, we can model it with a polynomial; we formulate the single-feature case. This is often called non-linear regression, but it is more accurately described as linear-in-parameters regression. It also brings us back to overfitting.

Definition: The polynomial model

With d=1d=1d=1 and a scalar input xxx,
f^(x,θ)=θ0+θ1x+θ2x2+⋯+θMxM=∑i=0Mθixi=g(x)⊤θ,g(x)=[1, x, x2, …, xM]⊤.\hat f(x,\theta)=\theta_0+\theta_1x+\theta_2x^2+\cdots+\theta_Mx^M=\sum_{i=0}^M\theta_ix^i=g(x)^\top\theta, \qquad g(x)=\big[1,\ x,\ x^2,\ \dots,\ x^M\big]^\top .f^​(x,θ)=θ0​+θ1​x+θ2​x2+⋯+θM​xM=i=0∑M​θi​xi=g(x)⊤θ,g(x)=[1, x, x2, …, xM]⊤.
MMM is the degree, and there are M+1M+1M+1 coefficients. MMM is a hyper-parameter that controls the complexity of the model; M=1M=1M=1 is linear regression and M=0M=0M=0 is a constant (the mean).

The model is linear in the parameters θ\thetaθ, and that is all the least-squares derivation used. The feature map g(x)g(x)g(x) may contain any fixed functions of xxx, for instance g(x)=[1/x, sin⁡(2πx), x2, ex, …]⊤g(x)=\big[1/x,\ \sin(2\pi x),\ x^2,\ e^x,\ \dots\big]^\topg(x)=[1/x, sin(2πx), x2, ex, …]⊤. With nnn data points,
[e1⋮en]=[y1⋮yn]−[1x1x12⋯x1M⋮⋮⋮⋮1xnxn2⋯xnM]⏟X (a Vandermonde matrix)[θ0⋮θM],e=y−Xθ,θ=(X⊤X)−1X⊤y.\begin{bmatrix}e_1\\ \vdots\\ e_n\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}y_1\\ \vdots\\ y_n\end{bmatrix}- \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1&x_1&x_1^2&\cdots&x_1^M\\ \vdots&\vdots&\vdots&&\vdots\\1&x_n&x_n^2&\cdots&x_n^M\end{bmatrix}}_{X\ (\text{a Vandermonde matrix})} \begin{bmatrix}\theta_0\\ \vdots\\ \theta_M\end{bmatrix}, \qquad e=y-X\theta,\qquad \theta=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y .​e1​⋮en​​​=​y1​⋮yn​​​−X (a Vandermonde matrix)​1⋮1​x1​⋮xn​​x12​⋮xn2​​⋯⋯​x1M​⋮xnM​​​​​​θ0​⋮θM​​​,e=y−Xθ,θ=(X⊤X)−1X⊤y.
As the slide puts it, we have seen this before and are capable of solving it.

Common trap: "Linear" means linear in the parameters

y=w0+w1sin⁡x+w2exy=w_0+w_1\sin x+w_2e^xy=w0​+w1​sinx+w2​ex is linear regression. y=w0+ew1xy=w_0+e^{w_1x}y=w0​+ew1​x is not, because w1w_1w1​ sits inside the exponential. A curve in xxx becomes a straight line in the space of the new features: plotting yyy against z=x2z=x^2z=x2, for example.

Remember

Polynomial regression is linear regression on the features 1,x,…,xM1,x,\dots,x^M1,x,…,xM: the normal equations are unchanged, only XXX is wider, and MMM is a hyper-parameter.

#7. Underfitting, overfitting — the Bishop sine example

🧩Background you needwhy more parameters can be worse

Counting. A line has 2 parameters, a cubic 4, a degree-9 polynomial 10. With 10 data points, a degree-9 polynomial has as many knobs as there are points, so it can pass exactly through every point — including through the random noise.

Why that is bad. The noise is different every time you collect data. A curve that has bent itself to fit this particular noise will be wrong on the next data set. A simpler curve cannot chase the noise, so it captures only the real trend.

Bias and variance in plain words.

  • Bias: being wrong on average because the model is too simple (a straight line through a curved trend).
  • Variance: being unstable — the fitted curve changes a lot if the data change a little — because the model is too flexible.

The set-up (Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, §1.1). The process is f(x)=sin⁡(2πx)f(x)=\sin(2\pi x)f(x)=sin(2πx), the observations are y=f(x)+ny=f(x)+ny=f(x)+n at n=10n=10n=10 points, and the model is f^(x,θ)=θ0+θ1x+⋯+θMxM\hat f(x,\theta)=\theta_0+\theta_1x+\cdots+\theta_Mx^Mf^​(x,θ)=θ0​+θ1​x+⋯+θM​xM. If MMM is not known, how do we choose it?

  • With M=0M=0M=0 or M=1M=1M=1 the fit is a flat or tilted line: underfitting, because the model is too simple.
  • With M=3M=3M=3 the fit follows the sine curve well.
  • With M=9M=9M=9 the residual error is zero — y=f^(x,θ)y=\hat f(x,\theta)y=f^​(x,θ) at every data point — but the curve oscillates wildly and is nothing like the true function. This is overfitting: the model is too complex and fits the data rather than the true function.

The coefficients explode as MMM grows (slide table):

M=0M=0M=0 M=1M=1M=1 M=3M=3M=3 M=9M=9M=9
θ0\theta_0θ0​ 0.190.190.19 0.820.820.82 0.310.310.31 0.350.350.35
θ1\theta_1θ1​ −1.27-1.27−1.27 7.997.997.99 232.37232.37232.37
θ2\theta_2θ2​ −25.43-25.43−25.43 −5321.83-5321.83−5321.83
θ3\theta_3θ3​ 17.3717.3717.37 48 568.3148\,568.3148568.31
θ4,…,θ9\theta_4,\dots,\theta_9θ4​,…,θ9​ −231 639.30-231\,639.30−231639.30, 640 042.26640\,042.26640042.26, −1 061 800.52-1\,061\,800.52−1061800.52, 1 042 400.181\,042\,400.181042400.18, −557 682.99-557\,682.99−557682.99, 125 201.43125\,201.43125201.43

A puzzle. The cubic is a special case of the degree-9 polynomial (set θ4=⋯=θ9=0\theta_4=\cdots=\theta_9=0θ4​=⋯=θ9​=0), so why does M=9M=9M=9 perform worse? Because ten coefficients are tuned to ten data points, and least squares spends the extra freedom fitting the noise, with enormous coefficients that cancel one another between the data points.

How can we detect overfitting without knowing the true function? The slides give three remedies.

  • Solution 1 — a train/validation split. Overfitting shows up as poor generalisation: a large error on validation or test data. Plotting ERMSE_{\mathrm{RMS}}ERMS​ against MMM, the training error falls all the way to zero at M=9M=9M=9, while the validation error falls until about M=3M=3M=3, stays flat up to M=8M=8M=8 and then shoots up at M=9M=9M=9. A good choice is therefore around M=3M=3M=3. (Training error can never be used to choose MMM: it always prefers the most complex model.) With very little data, use leave-one-out validation; for the four customers the leave-one-out RMSE is 1.491.491.49 for M=0M=0M=0, 1.061.061.06 for M=1M=1M=1 and 3.573.573.57 for M=2M=2M=2, so the line wins.
  • Solution 2 — more data. The degree-9 fit oscillates with n=10n=10n=10 points, settles down with n=15n=15n=15, and lies almost on top of sin⁡(2πx)\sin(2\pi x)sin(2πx) with n=100n=100n=100. We overfitted because we did not have enough data for that many parameters. (MMM plays the role that kkk plays in kNN: it controls the complexity of the model, and fixing M=3M=3M=3 restricts the number of parameters.)
  • Solution 3 — regularization (§9).
Definition: Underfitting and overfitting

Underfitting: the model is too simple, and its error is large on both the training data and new data (high bias). Overfitting: the model fits the noise, with a tiny training error and a large error on new data (high variance). With nnn distinct inputs, zero training error is guaranteed as soon as M≥n−1M\ge n-1M≥n−1; this proves only that the model can memorise.

Theorem / Key result: Bias and variance (outline Week 5; PSet 5 P8; PSet 6 P1)

The expected test error decomposes as
Bias2+Variance+Noise(L01).\text{Bias}^2+\text{Variance}+\text{Noise}\qquad(\text{L01}).Bias2+Variance+Noise(L01).
More flexible models — a higher degree MMM, a smaller penalty λ\lambdaλ, a smaller kkk — have lower bias and higher variance.

In PSet 5, Problem 8, a linear and a cubic model are fitted to 100100100 points. The cubic's training error is always at most the linear model's, whatever the truth, because the models are nested. If the truth is linear, we expect the linear model to have the lower test error, since the extra cubic terms add variance without reducing bias. If the truth is non-linear by an unknown amount, the comparison of test errors cannot be decided in advance; it must be settled with validation data.

Remember

Training error always falls as complexity grows, so choose MMM (or λ\lambdaλ, or kkk) on validation data; underfitting means too simple, and overfitting means memorised noise with exploding coefficients.

#8. The closed form in practice

  • Do not compute the inverse. Forming X⊤XX^\top XX⊤X squares the sensitivity of the problem to rounding error. Software solves least squares with stable factorisations instead; np.linalg.lstsq(X, y) returns (7.186, −0.1017)(7.186,\,-0.1017)(7.186,−0.1017) for the age data.
  • Scale your features. Raw ages turn the loss surface into a long, thin valley. Centring the ages makes X⊤X=diag⁡(4, 368.75)X^\top X=\operatorname{diag}(4,\,368.75)X⊤X=diag(4,368.75), and the condition number — which measures how much errors in the input are magnified in the solution — falls from about 21 00021\,00021000 to about 929292. For a cubic in raw age the condition number is about 9×10139\times10^{13}9×1013; after standardising, z=(x−36.25)/9.60z=(x-36.25)/9.60z=(x−36.25)/9.60, it is about 808080. Standardising is essential for polynomial features.
  • Cost. Forming X⊤XX^\top XX⊤X takes about n(d+1)2n(d+1)^2n(d+1)2 operations and solving the system about (d+1)3(d+1)^3(d+1)3. This is instantaneous for hundreds of features but impractical for millions, where iterative methods such as gradient descent (L09) take over. Linear regression is one of the few models with an analytical solution.
  • The battery problem. Features such as cycle count, temperature and charge rate feed a linear model; polynomial features capture non-linear degradation; whole batteries are held out for validation; and one standardises, uses lstsq, and reports the RMSE in cycles.

"So far and moving forward" (slide p28). We assumed a linear structure; the number of parameters is the dimension of the feature space plus one; the loss was built from the residual error; and the optimisation problem has an analytical solution. A numerical algorithm comes next.

#9. Regularization

🧩Background you needwhat a penalty does

Think of the loss as a price to be minimised. Regularisation adds a second price: a charge for having large weights.
total price=how badly we fit the data⏟squared error+λ×how large the weights are⏟penalty.\text{total price}=\underbrace{\text{how badly we fit the data}}_{\text{squared error}}+\lambda\times\underbrace{\text{how large the weights are}}_{\text{penalty}} .total price=squared errorhow badly we fit the data​​+λ×penaltyhow large the weights are​​.
The number λ≥0\lambda\ge0λ≥0 is the exchange rate between the two:

  • λ=0\lambda=0λ=0: weights are free, and we get ordinary least squares.
  • λ\lambdaλ huge: weights are very expensive, so the best choice is weights near zero (a flat line).
  • In between: the model fits the data, but only as tightly as it can afford.

Since overfitted models have enormous weights (look at the M=9M=9M=9 table), charging for large weights stops them from overfitting.

Overview. Regularization encourages the coefficients to be small by adding a penalty term (a regulariser) to the error:
minimizeθLreg(θ)=L(θ)+λ R(θ),whereL(θ)=12∥y−Xθ∥22.\underset{\theta}{\text{minimize}}\quad \mathcal L_{\mathrm{reg}}(\theta)=\mathcal L(\theta)+\lambda\,\mathcal R(\theta),\qquad\text{where}\quad \mathcal L(\theta)=\tfrac12\|y-X\theta\|_2^2 .θminimize​Lreg​(θ)=L(θ)+λR(θ),whereL(θ)=21​∥y−Xθ∥22​.
The parameter λ≥0\lambda\ge0λ≥0 sets the trade-off between the regulariser and the original loss. With λ=0\lambda=0λ=0 we recover ordinary least squares (OLS); as λ→∞\lambda\to\inftyλ→∞ every slope is driven to zero and the model becomes the constant yˉ\bar yyˉ​. Regularization treats three symptoms of a single disease — too much freedom for the amount of data: memorised noise, exploding coefficients, and a singular X⊤XX^\top XX⊤X.

#9a. Ridge regression (L2L^2L2 / ℓ2\ell^2ℓ2 penalty)

Definition: Ridge regression

With R(θ)=12∥θ∥22\mathcal R(\theta)=\tfrac12\|\theta\|_2^2R(θ)=21​∥θ∥22​,
minimizeθLreg(θ)=12∥y−Xθ∥22+λ2∥θ∥22.\underset{\theta}{\text{minimize}}\quad \mathcal L_{\mathrm{reg}}(\theta)=\tfrac12\|y-X\theta\|_2^2+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\|\theta\|_2^2 .θminimize​Lreg​(θ)=21​∥y−Xθ∥22​+2λ​∥θ∥22​.
The penalty trades off the fit of the model to the data (the first term is large if the model fits poorly) against the squared norm of the coefficients (the second term is large if the coefficients are large); a large λ\lambdaλ penalises the coefficients more. Intuitively, we minimise the error while keeping the norm of the coefficients bounded. In deep learning the same penalty is called weight decay.

Derivation: The closed form (slide p41; 2025 Mid P7a)

The regularised loss is still quadratic, so it has a closed-form minimiser. Its gradient is
∇Lreg(θ)=12(−2X⊤y+2X⊤Xθ+2λθ)=X⊤Xθ+λθ−X⊤y.\nabla\mathcal L_{\mathrm{reg}}(\theta)=\tfrac12\big(-2X^\top y+2X^\top X\theta+2\lambda\theta\big)=X^\top X\theta+\lambda\theta-X^\top y .∇Lreg​(θ)=21​(−2X⊤y+2X⊤Xθ+2λθ)=X⊤Xθ+λθ−X⊤y.
Setting it equal to zero,
X⊤Xθ+λθ=X⊤y⟹(X⊤X+λI) θ=X⊤y⟹  θ(λ)=(X⊤X+λI)−1X⊤y  X^\top X\theta+\lambda\theta=X^\top y\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad (X^\top X+\lambda I)\,\theta=X^\top y\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \boxed{\;\theta(\lambda)=(X^\top X+\lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y\;}X⊤Xθ+λθ=X⊤y⟹(X⊤X+λI)θ=X⊤y⟹θ(λ)=(X⊤X+λI)−1X⊤y​
At λ=0\lambda=0λ=0 this is the unregularised solution; as λ→∞\lambda\to\inftyλ→∞ it tends to the zero vector. The only change from OLS is the addition of λ\lambdaλ to the diagonal of X⊤XX^\top XX⊤X — the "ridge" that gives the method its name.

wridge=19[6−3−33][35]=19[18−15−9+15]=[1/32/3].w_{\mathrm{ridge}}=\frac19\begin{bmatrix}6&-3\\-3&3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3\\5\end{bmatrix}=\frac19\begin{bmatrix}18-15\\-9+15\end{bmatrix}=\boxed{\begin{bmatrix}1/3\\2/3\end{bmatrix}}.wridge​=91​[6−3​−33​][35​]=91​[18−15−9+15​]=[1/32/3​]​.
(c) As λ\lambdaλ increases, the penalty pushes the coefficients towards zero, increasing the bias and reducing the variance; in the limit λ→∞\lambda\to\inftyλ→∞, wridge→0w_{\mathrm{ridge}}\to\mathbf 0wridge​→0. (For comparison, OLS fits these two points exactly with w=(0,1)w=(0,1)w=(0,1).)

Common trap: Leave the intercept alone

Penalising the intercept w0w_0w0​ would pull every prediction towards zero — a point fixed by the units of measurement rather than by the data. Either use λD\lambda DλD with D=diag⁡(0,1,…,1)D=\operatorname{diag}(0,1,\dots,1)D=diag(0,1,…,1), or centre the features and yyy and apply λI\lambda IλI to the slopes only. Note that the textbook formula (X⊤X+λI)−1X⊤y(X^\top X+\lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y(X⊤X+λI)−1X⊤y, applied to an XXX that contains the column of ones, does penalise the intercept; the 2025 Mid used it that way, so follow the loss as the question states it.

Theorem / Key result: Ridge always has a unique solution

For λ>0\lambda>0λ>0 and every v≠0v\neq\mathbf 0v=0,
v⊤(X⊤X+λI)v=∥Xv∥22+λ∥v∥22 ≥ λ∥v∥22 > 0,v^\top\big(X^\top X+\lambda I\big)v=\|Xv\|_2^2+\lambda\|v\|_2^2\ \ge\ \lambda\|v\|_2^2\ >\ 0 ,v⊤(X⊤X+λI)v=∥Xv∥22​+λ∥v∥22​ ≥ λ∥v∥22​ > 0,
so (X⊤X+λI)v(X^\top X+\lambda I)v(X⊤X+λI)v can never be the zero vector. The matrix is therefore invertible and the minimiser is unique, even when d>nd>nd>n or when columns are exact duplicates.

With an exact duplicate feature, ridge splits the weight equally: swapping the two weights leaves both the fit and the penalty unchanged, and the minimiser is unique, so the two weights must be equal. In PSet 6, Problem 2, with identical features xi1=xi2x_{i1}=x_{i2}xi1​=xi2​,
w1⋆=w2⋆=2ay14a2+λ,which equals 0.8 for a=1, y1=2, λ=1.w_1^\star=w_2^\star=\frac{2ay_1}{4a^2+\lambda},\qquad\text{which equals }0.8\text{ for }a=1,\ y_1=2,\ \lambda=1 .w1⋆​=w2⋆​=4a2+λ2ay1​​,which equals 0.8 for a=1, y1​=2, λ=1.

Irrelevant features receive small but non-zero weights in the ridge solution, whereas ideally we would like to give them zero weight — which is what the lasso achieves.

Common trap: Standardise before you penalise

Penalties are not unit-free. If age is recorded in months rather than years, the same λ=100\lambda=100λ=100 hardly shrinks the slope at all (−0.1015-0.1015−0.1015 per year instead of −0.08-0.08−0.08), because the slope's numerical value becomes twelve times smaller and its penalty 144144144 times cheaper. Income in rupees (values near 10510^5105) receives a tiny weight whose penalty is negligible, while "number of children" pays in full. Standardise the features, using training-set statistics, and leave the intercept unpenalised.

#9b. Lasso regression (L1L^1L1 / ℓ1\ell^1ℓ1 penalty)

Definition: The lasso

With R(θ)=∥θ∥1=∑i∣θi∣\mathcal R(\theta)=\|\theta\|_1=\sum_i|\theta_i|R(θ)=∥θ∥1​=∑i​∣θi​∣,
minimizeθLreg(θ)=12∥y−Xθ∥22+λ∥θ∥1.\underset{\theta}{\text{minimize}}\quad \mathcal L_{\mathrm{reg}}(\theta)=\tfrac12\|y-X\theta\|_2^2+\lambda\|\theta\|_1 .θminimize​Lreg​(θ)=21​∥y−Xθ∥22​+λ∥θ∥1​.
The name stands for least absolute shrinkage and selection operator. Graphically, the constraint region is a diamond, and the error contours typically meet it at a corner. Every corner lies on an axis, where some coefficients are exactly zero, so the lasso gives a sparse solution. In short: ridge shrinks, the lasso selects.

Why absolute values produce exact zeros: soft thresholding. For a single centred feature, write a=∑ixi2a=\sum_ix_i^2a=∑i​xi2​ and b=∑ixiyib=\sum_ix_iy_ib=∑i​xi​yi​. Up to a constant, the lasso loss is
f(w)=a2w2−bw+λ∣w∣.f(w)=\frac a2w^2-bw+\lambda|w| .f(w)=2a​w2−bw+λ∣w∣.
Consider the three possible locations of the minimum.

  • If it lies at some w>0w>0w>0, then f′(w)=aw−b+λ=0f'(w)=aw-b+\lambda=0f′(w)=aw−b+λ=0, so w=(b−λ)/aw=(b-\lambda)/aw=(b−λ)/a, which is positive only when b>λb>\lambdab>λ.
  • If it lies at some w<0w<0w<0, then f′(w)=aw−b−λ=0f'(w)=aw-b-\lambda=0f′(w)=aw−b−λ=0, so w=(b+λ)/aw=(b+\lambda)/aw=(b+λ)/a, which is negative only when b<−λb<-\lambdab<−λ.
  • Otherwise, when ∣b∣≤λ|b|\le\lambda∣b∣≤λ, the minimum is at the kink w=0w=0w=0: just to the right of 000 the slope −b+λ-b+\lambda−b+λ is non-negative, and just to the left the slope −b−λ-b-\lambda−b−λ is non-positive, so both directions lead uphill.

The three cases combine into one formula, which we set beside its ridge and OLS counterparts:
wlasso⋆=S(b,λ)a,S(b,λ)=sign⁡(b)max⁡(∣b∣−λ, 0);wridge⋆=ba+λ;wOLS⋆=ba.w^\star_{\mathrm{lasso}}=\frac{S(b,\lambda)}{a},\quad S(b,\lambda)=\operatorname{sign}(b)\max\big(|b|-\lambda,\,0\big); \qquad w^\star_{\mathrm{ridge}}=\frac{b}{a+\lambda}; \qquad w^\star_{\mathrm{OLS}}=\frac{b}{a}.wlasso⋆​=aS(b,λ)​,S(b,λ)=sign(b)max(∣b∣−λ,0);wridge⋆​=a+λb​;wOLS⋆​=ab​.
OLS divides the evidence bbb by aaa. Ridge enlarges the denominator, shrinking every weight by the same factor. The lasso subtracts λ\lambdaλ from the evidence, shrinking every weight by the same amount, and sets to exactly zero any weight whose evidence satisfies ∣b∣≤λ|b|\le\lambda∣b∣≤λ.

Worked example: One weight by hand

Take a=2a=2a=2, b=5b=5b=5 and λ=6\lambda=6λ=6. Then
wOLS=52=2.5,wridge=52+6=0.625,wlasso=S(5,6)2=0,w_{\mathrm{OLS}}=\frac52=2.5,\qquad w_{\mathrm{ridge}}=\frac{5}{2+6}=0.625,\qquad w_{\mathrm{lasso}}=\frac{S(5,6)}{2}=0,wOLS​=25​=2.5,wridge​=2+65​=0.625,wlasso​=2S(5,6)​=0,
since ∣5∣≤6|5|\le6∣5∣≤6; the lasso weight is zero for every λ≥5\lambda\ge5λ≥5. For the age data, w1(λ)=−max⁡(37.5−λ,0)/368.75w_1(\lambda)=-\max(37.5-\lambda,0)/368.75w1​(λ)=−max(37.5−λ,0)/368.75, which reaches zero at λ=37.5\lambda=37.5λ=37.5.

Many weights. There is no closed form. Coordinate descent cycles through the features, updating each weight by soft thresholding with the others held fixed,
wj ← S(xj⊤r(j), λ)xj⊤xj,r(j)=y−∑k≠jxkwk,w_j\ \leftarrow\ \frac{S\big(x_j^\top r^{(j)},\,\lambda\big)}{x_j^\top x_j},\qquad r^{(j)}=y-\sum_{k\neq j}x_kw_k ,wj​ ← xj⊤​xj​S(xj⊤​r(j),λ)​,r(j)=y−k=j∑​xk​wk​,
and, because the lasso loss is convex, it converges to the global minimum. Lasso optimisation is computationally more expensive than ridge. On the standardised age and sleep features, the sleep weight drops out exactly at λ≈0.40\lambda\approx0.40λ≈0.40 and the age weight at λ=3.906\lambda=3.906λ=3.906, whereas ridge keeps both. In a simulated example with twelve features of which three matter, the lasso set five of the nine useless weights exactly to zero and predicted best.

Worked example: Lasso versus ridge (2024 Mid, Problem 5)

(a) The lasso penalises ∥θ∥1\|\theta\|_1∥θ∥1​ and can shrink some coefficients exactly to zero, producing a sparse model that selects features. Ridge penalises ∥θ∥22\|\theta\|_2^2∥θ∥22​ and shrinks coefficients towards zero, but not exactly to zero, so it keeps every feature with reduced influence.

(b) The lasso loss is L(θ)=12∥Aθ−y∥2+λ∥θ∥1\mathcal L(\theta)=\tfrac12\|A\theta-y\|^2+\lambda\|\theta\|_1L(θ)=21​∥Aθ−y∥2+λ∥θ∥1​. The L1L^1L1 penalty is not differentiable at zero; it has a sharp corner there, which makes it likely that the optimum sets coefficients exactly to zero.

(c) Increasing λ\lambdaλ strengthens the penalty and drives more coefficients to zero, increasing sparsity; decreasing it keeps more features. The value of λ\lambdaλ balances complexity against sparsity.

#9c. Elastic net and comparison

Definition: The elastic net: a hybrid of L1L^1L1 and L2L^2L2

minimizeθLreg(θ)=12∥y−Xθ∥22+λ1∥θ∥1+λ22∥θ∥22.\underset{\theta}{\text{minimize}}\quad \mathcal L_{\mathrm{reg}}(\theta)=\tfrac12\|y-X\theta\|_2^2+\lambda_1\|\theta\|_1+\tfrac{\lambda_2}{2}\|\theta\|_2^2 .θminimize​Lreg​(θ)=21​∥y−Xθ∥22​+λ1​∥θ∥1​+2λ2​​∥θ∥22​.
Ridge and the lasso are special cases. The elastic net combines their strengths — it selects features like the lasso while keeping groups of correlated features together like ridge — at the cost of two hyper-parameters, λ1\lambda_1λ1​ and λ2\lambda_2λ2​, both tuned on validation data.

Ridge, λ2∥w∥22\tfrac\lambda2\|w\|_2^22λ​∥w∥22​ Lasso, λ∥w∥1\lambda\|w\|_1λ∥w∥1​
penalty error + λ×+\ \lambda\times+ λ× sum of squares of the coefficients error + λ×+\ \lambda\times+ λ× sum of absolute values
solution closed form (X⊤X+λI)−1X⊤y(X^\top X+\lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y(X⊤X+λI)−1X⊤y iterative (coordinate descent), more expensive
effect on weights shrinks all by a factor; none exactly zero shrinks by an amount; many exactly zero (sparse, and therefore biased)
geometry a disc (round) a diamond (corners on the axes)
uniqueness always unique for λ>0\lambda>0λ>0 can fail with perfectly correlated features
correlated features spreads the weight across them tends to pick one
best when many features each contribute a little a few features matter

Mid MCQs on this material: the regulariser that promotes a sparse weight vector is the L1L^1L1 penalty (2024, MCQ 9); the diamond figure shows a sparse, L1L^1L1-penalised solution, not ridge (MCQ 14). For ridge with λ>0\lambda>0λ>0 (2025, MCQ 21): the closed form is correct, and coefficients shrink as λ\lambdaλ grows; but ridge does not set coefficients exactly to zero, and it decreases variance at the cost of bias, rather than increasing it. The bias–variance trade-off is controlled by λ\lambdaλ and by the polynomial degree (2024, MCQ 6). Variance is reduced by adding more data or by lowering model complexity (2024, MCQ 5).

🔍Where does this come from?why the gradient of λ2∥θ∥2\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\|\theta\|^22λ​∥θ∥2 is λθ\lambda\thetaλθ

Write the penalty out: λ2∥θ∥2=λ2(θ12+θ22+⋯+θd2)\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\|\theta\|^2=\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\big(\theta_1^2+\theta_2^2+\cdots+\theta_d^2\big)2λ​∥θ∥2=2λ​(θ12​+θ22​+⋯+θd2​).

Its partial derivative with respect to θk\theta_kθk​ uses only the θk2\theta_k^2θk2​ term:
∂∂θk λ2θk2=λ2⋅2θk=λθk.\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta_k}\,\frac{\lambda}{2}\theta_k^2=\frac{\lambda}{2}\cdot2\theta_k=\lambda\theta_k .∂θk​∂​2λ​θk2​=2λ​⋅2θk​=λθk​.
Stacking over kkk gives the vector λθ\lambda\thetaλθ. Adding this to the least-squares gradient,
X⊤Xθ−X⊤y+λθ=0⟹(X⊤X+λI)θ=X⊤y.X^\top X\theta-X^\top y+\lambda\theta=\mathbf 0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad (X^\top X+\lambda I)\theta=X^\top y .X⊤Xθ−X⊤y+λθ=0⟹(X⊤X+λI)θ=X⊤y.
The step X⊤Xθ+λθ=(X⊤X+λI)θX^\top X\theta+\lambda\theta=(X^\top X+\lambda I)\thetaX⊤Xθ+λθ=(X⊤X+λI)θ uses λθ=λIθ\lambda\theta=\lambda I\thetaλθ=λIθ: multiplying by the identity changes nothing, and writing it this way lets us factor out θ\thetaθ.

🔍Where does this come from?why the lasso sets weights exactly to zero (the slope argument)

For one weight the lasso minimises f(w)=a2w2−bw+λ∣w∣f(w)=\tfrac a2w^2-bw+\lambda|w|f(w)=2a​w2−bw+λ∣w∣. The term ∣w∣|w|∣w∣ has a corner at w=0w=0w=0: its slope is −1-1−1 just to the left of 000 and +1+1+1 just to the right.

  • Just to the right of 000, the slope of fff is −b+λ-b+\lambda−b+λ.
  • Just to the left of 000, it is −b−λ-b-\lambda−b−λ.

If ∣b∣≤λ|b|\le\lambda∣b∣≤λ, the right-hand slope is ≥0\ge0≥0 (uphill to the right) and the left-hand slope is ≤0\le0≤0 (uphill to the left). So w=0w=0w=0 is the bottom of the valley — exactly zero. A smooth penalty like w2w^2w2 has slope 000 at w=0w=0w=0 and no corner, so it can never pin the weight there; it only shrinks it.

Example. a=2a=2a=2, b=5b=5b=5: with λ=6\lambda=6λ=6 we have ∣b∣=5≤6|b|=5\le6∣b∣=5≤6, so the lasso weight is 000; with λ=1\lambda=1λ=1 it is (5−1)/2=2(5-1)/2=2(5−1)/2=2.

#10. Choosing λ\lambdaλ

🧩Background you needvalidation and cross-validation, recapped

Why not choose λ\lambdaλ by training error? Training error is smallest when there is no penalty at all, so it would always pick λ=0\lambda=0λ=0 — the overfitting choice.

Validation. Hold some data back. Fit the model with each candidate λ\lambdaλ on the rest, and see which λ\lambdaλ predicts the held-back data best.

kkk-fold cross-validation does this kkk times, each time holding back a different slice, and averages the results — so every data point gets a turn at being the "unseen" data. Leave-one-out is the extreme case where each slice is a single point.

  • Never on training error, which always selects λ=0\lambda=0λ=0.
  • Leave-one-out validation on very small data sets. For the four customers (standardised age, unpenalised intercept), the leave-one-out RMSE is:
λ\lambdaλ 000 0.10.10.1 0.30.30.3 111 333 101010
line (M=1M=1M=1) 1.061.061.06 1.051.051.05 1.031.031.03 1.041.041.04 1.151.151.15 1.331.331.33
parabola (M=2M=2M=2) 3.573.573.57 1.981.981.98 1.251.251.25 1.061.061.06 1.201.201.20 1.351.351.35
cubic (M=3M=3M=3) — 1.771.771.77 1.601.601.60 1.381.381.38 1.291.291.29 1.321.321.32

Regularisation rescues the parabola dramatically and makes the cubic usable, but the best model is still a lightly penalised line: four customers cannot support a curve. Degree and penalty are chosen together.

  • kkk-fold cross-validation in practice: choose a grid of λ\lambdaλ values evenly spaced in ln⁡λ\ln\lambdalnλ; for each, fit on k−1k-1k−1 folds and validate on the remaining one, then average; select the best λ\lambdaλ, refit on all the training data, and report performance on the untouched test set. Compute the standardisation inside each fold, and split grouped data by group.
  • Implementation. Ridge is OLS on augmented data,
    X~=[X0   λ Id],y~=[y0],\tilde X=\begin{bmatrix}X\\ 0\ \ \ \sqrt\lambda\,I_d\end{bmatrix},\qquad \tilde y=\begin{bmatrix}y\\ \mathbf 0\end{bmatrix},X~=[X0   λ​Id​​],y~​=[y0​],
    that is, ddd imaginary customers who each pull one slope towards zero, solved with lstsq. A gradient step for ridge multiplies the weights by (1−ηλ)(1-\eta\lambda)(1−ηλ), which is why it is called weight decay. In probabilistic terms, ridge corresponds to a Gaussian prior on the weights and the lasso to a Laplace prior (maximum a posteriori estimation, L13).

Remember: The one line for this lecture

Least squares solves X⊤Xw=X⊤yX^\top Xw=X^\top yX⊤Xw=X⊤y — the residual is orthogonal to the column space, equivalently the gradient is zero; polynomial regression is the same machine with features xkx^kxk and overfits when MMM is large; and regularization adds λ\lambdaλ times the size of www: ridge, (X⊤X+λI)−1X⊤y(X^\top X+\lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y(X⊤X+λI)−1X⊤y, shrinks smoothly and is always solvable, while the corners of the lasso's diamond give sparse solutions — with every hyper-parameter chosen on validation data, never on training error.
